title: Passwords
subtitle: Weak or reused passwords are the single most common cause of account compromise. This guide covers everything from creating strong passwords to setting up the most secure forms of multi-factor authentication.

context.title: Why this guide matters
context.body: If someone gains access to your email or banking account, they can reset passwords across every other account you own. Password security is the foundation everything else rests on - and it's one of the easiest things to meaningfully improve.
context.body2: The good news: a password manager does most of the heavy lifting. Once you have one set up, strong and unique passwords require almost no extra effort on your part.

items.name: Use long, complex passwords (16+ characters)
items.why: Password cracking tools can test billions of combinations per second. An 8-character password can be brute-forced in hours. A randomly generated 16-character password with mixed characters would take centuries with current technology. Length matters far more than complexity alone.

steps.text: For passwords you need to memorize (like your password manager master password), create a passphrase with 4-5 words plus a number and symbol. Example: `correct-horse-battery-staple7!`
For everything else, let your password manager generate a random password of at least 16 characters with uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols
Never use personal information in passwords - birthdays, names, pet names, or addresses are easy to guess or find through data breaches
Check if any of your passwords have appeared in known data breaches at `haveibeenpwned.com`

items.name: Never reuse passwords across accounts
items.why: When a company suffers a data breach, attackers immediately try stolen credentials on other major services - email, banking, social media. This is called credential stuffing. If you reuse passwords, one breach compromises all of them. Billions of username/password combinations from past breaches are freely available online.

steps.text: Every single account should have a different password - no exceptions for 'unimportant' sites. Even a low-stakes account can be used to reset passwords elsewhere
Use a password manager to generate and store unique passwords - there's no need to memorize them
Visit `haveibeenpwned.com` and enter your email addresses to see which breaches have exposed your credentials - then update those passwords immediately

items.name: Set up a dedicated password manager
items.why: Browser-saved passwords are riskier - they can be exported or accessed by malware, and they're tied to your Google or Apple account. A dedicated password manager encrypts your vault locally before syncing, meaning the provider never has access to your passwords.

steps.text: Pick a password manager - `Bitwarden` (free, open source) or `1Password` (paid, excellent UI) are the top recommendations
Create an account and set a strong master password - this is the one password you must memorize. Use a long passphrase. Write it down somewhere physically secure until you've memorized it
Install the browser extension and mobile app
Import any passwords saved in your browser: in Chrome go to `Settings → Passwords → Export`, then import the file into your password manager
As you log into sites going forward, let the password manager save and auto-fill credentials. Gradually update old weak or reused passwords using the manager's built-in generator

items.name: Enable passkeys wherever supported
items.path: Account security settings on supported sites
items.why: Passkeys use public-key cryptography - a unique key pair is generated for each site, and your private key never leaves your device. They cannot be phished, cannot be leaked in a data breach, and don't require you to type anything. They're resistant to every major attack vector that threatens traditional passwords.

steps.text: When a site offers 'Sign in with a passkey' or 'Create a passkey', always choose it over a traditional password
On iPhone: passkeys are saved to your iCloud Keychain automatically. On Android: they're saved to Google Password Manager or a third-party manager like Bitwarden
Major services that support passkeys include Google, Apple, Microsoft, GitHub, and PayPal. Check `passkeys.directory` for a full list
Even after enabling a passkey, keep a strong backup password in your password manager in case you need it

items.name: Set up a hardware security key (YubiKey)
items.path: Account security settings on supported sites
items.why: A hardware security key is a physical device that you plug in or tap to authenticate. Because the key must be physically present, remote attackers cannot access your account even if they have your password. It is completely immune to phishing - you cannot be tricked into handing over your second factor over the phone or via a fake website.

steps.text: Purchase a YubiKey from `yubico.com`. The YubiKey 5 NFC works with both USB-A and NFC for phones. Buy two - keep one as a backup
Register your key on your most critical accounts first: Google, Apple ID, Microsoft, GitHub, and your password manager
For Google: go to `myaccount.google.com → Security → 2-Step Verification → Add security key`
Store your backup key in a physically secure location - not with your primary key

items.name: Install an authenticator app and enable it everywhere
items.why: An authenticator app generates a time-based one-time code (TOTP) that changes every 30 seconds and is tied to your specific device. Even if an attacker has your username and password, they cannot log in without also having physical access to your phone. Unlike SMS codes, these cannot be intercepted via SIM swapping.

steps.text: Download `Proton Authenticator` (best privacy) or `Aegis` (Android, open source) or `Raivo` (iOS, open source)
On each account, go to `Security settings → Two-factor authentication → Authenticator app`
Scan the QR code shown with your authenticator app - this links the app to your account
Save the backup/recovery codes the site provides in your password manager vault
Enable on every account that supports it. Priority order: email → bank → password manager → Apple/Google account → social media

sections.label: MFA - SMS / email OTP (use as last resort)

items.name: Understand the risks of SMS-based MFA
items.path: Applies when SMS is your only MFA option
items.why: SMS codes are vulnerable to SIM swapping - where an attacker convinces your carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card they control. They then receive your MFA codes. This attack has been used to drain cryptocurrency accounts and take over high-value social media profiles.

steps.text: If a site only offers SMS MFA, enable it - it's still significantly better than no MFA at all
Whenever a site later adds authenticator app or hardware key support, switch to it immediately
Call your mobile carrier and ask them to add a PIN or passphrase requirement before any account changes can be made - this makes SIM swapping harder
Make sure notification previews are disabled on your lock screen so SMS codes aren't visible to anyone who picks up your phone

items.name: Secure your highest-value accounts first
items.why: Your email account is the master key to everything else - most password resets are sent there. Your Apple ID or Google account controls access to your phone, photos, and backups. Compromising either of these gives an attacker a foothold to take over your entire digital life.

steps.text: Priority 1 - Critical: `Email` (Gmail, ProtonMail). Controls password resets for every other account
Priority 2 - Critical: `Apple ID / Google account`. Controls your phone, backups, and app purchases
Priority 3 - Critical: `Password manager`. Controls access to all your other credentials
Priority 4 - High: `Banking & financial accounts`. Direct financial risk if compromised
Priority 5 - High: `Social media`. Identity theft and impersonation risk
Priority 6 - Medium: `Everything else`. Any account can be a stepping stone to higher-value ones
